```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
library(sciparseR)
ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "sciparseR")
```

Tables in clinical papers carry most of the numbers that matter, and they
are also where naive PDF extraction fails most often: spanning headers,
two level headers, footnote markers glued to labels, dashes for missing
values, and tables that continue on the next page. sciparseR stores a
table as cells and keeps all of this information.

## Detection

A table is found from its caption ("Table 2. ...") and the block of
aligned rows that follows, or from aligned rows alone when there is no
caption (status `possible`). Column boundaries come from the horizontal
intervals that the rows share; ruling lines found on the rendered page
mark spanning headers and the end of the header.

```{r}
doc <- sc_parse(ex("trial_tables.pdf"))
sc_tables(doc)[, c("table_id", "label", "page", "n_rows", "n_cols", "n_header_rows", "ruled", "method", "status")]
```

## Cells

```{r}
cells <- sc_table_cells(doc, "Table 1")
cells[, c("row", "col", "row_span", "col_span", "is_header", "text", "markers", "missing_token")]
```

Things to notice:

* "Treatment group" spans two columns (`col_span = 2`): the rule under it
  in the PDF says so. "Characteristic" and "P value" span both header rows
  (`row_span = 2`): the header cells below them are empty.
* The table has two header rows.
* The superscript "a" after "Diabetes, n (%)" is stored in `markers` and
  removed from `text`; the original is in `text_raw`.
* The dash in the BMI row is a `missing_token`, not a number and not an
  empty cell.

Each cell has its own box, so values can be highlighted on the page:

```{r}
cells[cells$row == 3, c("text", "x0", "y0", "x1", "y1")]
```

## Data frame and matrix views

`sc_table_to_dataframe()` builds column names from all header rows,
joined with `" | "`, so the spanning header is not lost:

```{r}
sc_table_to_dataframe(doc, "Table 1")
```

The matrix view puts spanning text in the first covered position, or in
every covered position with `fill_spans = TRUE`:

```{r}
sc_table_to_matrix(doc, "Table 1", fill_spans = TRUE)[1:2, ]
```

## Captions and footnotes

```{r}
sc_table_caption(doc, "Table 1")
sc_table_footnotes(doc, "Table 1")[, c("marker", "text")]
```

## Tables across pages

A table continued on the next page is joined only when it is certain: the
caption repeats the label and says "continued", and the columns match.
Otherwise the second part is kept as a separate table with
`continuation_status = "possible"`.

```{r}
fe <- sc_parse(ex("figure_equation.pdf"))
sc_tables(fe)[, c("table_id", "label", "page", "continuation_of", "continuation_status")]
nrow(sc_table_to_dataframe(fe, "Table 3"))
nrow(sc_table_to_dataframe(fe, "Table 3", join_continuations = FALSE))
```

## Export

```{r}
files <- sc_export_tables(doc, file.path(tempdir(), "tables"))
basename(files)
```

One CSV per table plus `cells.csv`, the long table that keeps spans,
header flags, markers and boxes, because a flat CSV cannot.

## Limits

The geometric method handles ruled and borderless tables whose columns
are aligned. Tables drawn as images, tables with rotated text and tables
whose columns are not aligned need a learned model; sciparseR does not
claim to handle them in this version (see `vignette("ocr-models-grobid")`).
For such tables, JATS XML from the publisher, when it exists, is the
better source.
